title: What are the Databricks cluster types — All-Purpose clusters (interactive, shared, for development), Job clusters (ephemeral, created/terminated per job run, for production), and SQL Warehouses (serverless/classic, for SQL analytics workloads) — and when do you use each?
shortTitle: What are the Databricks cluster types
topicTitle: What are the Databricks cluster types

s1_definition.profdef: Databricks offers three main compute types for different workloads. All-Purpose clusters are long-lived, shared, interactive clusters used for development and exploration in notebooks. Job clusters are ephemeral clusters that Databricks creates just before a scheduled job runs and tears down immediately after, giving each production job isolated, cost-efficient compute. SQL Warehouses are compute endpoints optimized specifically for SQL analytics and BI tools, available in classic and serverless flavors, where serverless starts almost instantly from a managed pool. You choose based on whether the work is interactive development, automated production, or SQL analytics.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India has three kinds of work vehicles. An All-Purpose cluster is like the staff pool car that sits in the lot all day, shared by several employees who hop in and out to run errands; it is convenient for ad hoc trips but costs money whenever it is parked and idling. A Job cluster is like hiring a dedicated delivery van that shows up exactly when a scheduled delivery is due, does that one delivery, and is returned the moment it is done, so you pay only for the trip and nobody else interferes with it. A SQL Warehouse is like a specialized armored cash-counting machine tuned for one job, counting money fast, that the reporting tellers plug into; the serverless version is already warmed up and ready the instant you flip the switch.
s1_definition.oneliner: All-Purpose clusters are shared and interactive for development, Job clusters are ephemeral and isolated for production jobs, and SQL Warehouses are tuned endpoints for SQL and BI, with serverless starting instantly.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Databricks offers three main compute types for different workloads. All-Purpose clusters are long-lived, shared, interactive clusters used for development and exploration in notebooks. Job clusters are ephemeral clusters that Databricks creates just before a scheduled job runs and tears down immediately after, giving each production job isolated, cost-efficient compute. SQL Warehouses are compute endpoints optimized specifically for SQL analytics and BI tools, available in classic and serverless flavors, where serverless starts almost instantly from a managed pool. You choose based on whether the work is interactive development, automated production, or SQL analytics.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India has three kinds of work vehicles. An All-Purpose cluster is like the staff pool car that sits in the lot all day, shared by several employees who hop in and out to run errands; it is convenient for ad hoc trips but costs money whenever it is parked and idling. A Job cluster is like hiring a dedicated delivery van that shows up exactly when a scheduled delivery is due, does that one delivery, and is returned the moment it is done, so you pay only for the trip and nobody else interferes with it. A SQL Warehouse is like a specialized armored cash-counting machine tuned for one job, counting money fast, that the reporting tellers plug into; the serverless version is already warmed up and ready the instant you flip the switch.

**One line to remember:** All-Purpose clusters are shared and interactive for development, Job clusters are ephemeral and isolated for production jobs, and SQL Warehouses are tuned endpoints for SQL and BI, with serverless starting instantly.

sections.s2_technical:
An All-Purpose cluster, formerly called an interactive cluster, is a cluster you start and keep running so that people can attach notebooks and run commands interactively. It is shared, meaning several users can work on the same cluster at once, and it stays alive until someone stops it or the auto-termination timer fires after an idle period. This is ideal for development, data exploration, debugging, and collaborative analysis, because starting a cluster takes minutes and you do not want to pay that startup cost for every cell you run. The downside is cost and noisy-neighbor effects: because it is long-lived and shared, an idle cluster wastes money and one user's heavy query can slow everyone on it, so you set a sensible auto-termination time and sometimes isolate heavy users.

A Job cluster is created automatically by the Databricks Jobs scheduler at the moment a scheduled job starts, runs only that job, and is terminated the instant the job finishes. Each job run gets its own fresh, isolated cluster, so production jobs do not interfere with each other or with interactive users, and you pay only for the exact duration of the run. This is the right choice for production pipelines: a nightly ETL, a scheduled model-training run, or a recurring report. Because the cluster is ephemeral and defined by the job configuration, runs are reproducible and clean, and there is no risk of leftover state from a previous session or an idle cluster quietly costing money. The small trade-off is the startup time per run, which is acceptable for scheduled batch work and is reduced by features like cluster pools that keep warm instances ready.

A SQL Warehouse, formerly called a SQL endpoint, is compute specialized for running SQL against the lakehouse, which is what BI tools and SQL analysts use. It runs the Photon engine and is tuned for concurrent SQL queries and dashboards rather than general Spark code. It comes in classic, where Databricks manages clusters in your cloud account, and serverless, where Databricks runs the compute in its own managed pool so a warehouse can start in seconds and scale concurrency automatically, which suits the bursty, many-users pattern of BI. You use a SQL Warehouse when the workload is SQL analytics, dashboards, and ad hoc SQL exploration, and you connect tools like Power BI, Tableau, or the Databricks SQL editor to it. A senior-level nuance is cost and governance control: serverless warehouses minimize idle cost and startup latency but run outside your cloud account's network boundary, which some regulated environments restrict, so banks sometimes choose classic warehouses inside their own network for sensitive data. Another nuance is matching compute to workload to control spend: using an always-on All-Purpose cluster for a nightly production job wastes money and risks interference, while using a Job cluster for interactive development frustrates users with repeated startup waits, so the discipline is development on All-Purpose, production on Job clusters, and SQL analytics on SQL Warehouses.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the data team used a single always-on All-Purpose cluster for everything: development, the nightly production ETL, and the analysts' BI queries. The result was a mess. The nightly ETL sometimes collided with a developer's heavy exploratory query and ran slowly, the cluster sat idle and expensive for large parts of the day, and when a developer accidentally left a huge job running it starved everyone. This is exactly the problem that choosing the right cluster type solves: different workloads need different compute lifecycles and isolation.

This is exactly how the cluster types differ. Interactive development belongs on a shared All-Purpose cluster with auto-termination, production jobs belong on ephemeral Job clusters that spin up and tear down per run so they are isolated and cost only for their runtime, and SQL analytics belongs on a SQL Warehouse tuned for concurrent queries.

Problem 2 — The analysts' dashboards were slow and bursty, with many users hitting them at nine in the morning and almost no use overnight, yet the cluster ran all night. A serverless SQL Warehouse that starts in seconds and scales concurrency to match the morning burst, while costing nothing overnight, fits this pattern far better. This is the serverless-versus-classic and workload-matching nuance.

Because we cannot run a real Databricks workspace, this runnable demo models the three cluster types and a router that picks the right one per workload, tracking cost and isolation. An `AllPurposeCluster` is long-lived and shared with an idle timer. A `JobCluster` is created per run and terminated after. A `SqlWarehouse` starts fast, in serverless mode nearly instantly, and serves concurrent SQL. A `ComputeRouter` dispatches a workload to the correct type and a `CostMeter` accumulates billed time. The demo routes a dev session, a nightly ETL, and a morning BI burst, showing isolation and the cost difference versus doing everything on one always-on cluster.

```
├── src/
│   ├── main/

│   │   │   ├── Workload.java               (type + work units + users)

│   │   │   ├── SqlWarehouse.java           (SQL endpoint, serverless/classic)
│   │   │   └── ComputeRouter.java          (picks the right type)
│   │   └── resources/
│   │       └── application.yml
│   └── test/
│       └── java/com/bank/compute/
│           └── ComputeRouterTest.java
```

Configuration file:

```yaml
# application.yml
compute:
  all-purpose:
    auto-termination-minutes: 30
  job-cluster:
    terminate-after-run: true
  sql-warehouse:
    mode: serverless          # serverless | classic
    startup-seconds: 5
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three workloads across a day: a developer exploration, a nightly production ETL, and a morning BI dashboard burst for forty users.

Step 1: The router sees the developer exploration is interactive development, so it routes it to the All-Purpose cluster. The cluster starts if needed, runs the small exploration shared by three users, and stays up afterward because interactive work benefits from a warm cluster.

Step 2: The All-Purpose cluster then sits idle. Because it is long-lived, it keeps billing during the idle window until the auto-termination timer fires at thirty minutes, at which point it terminates, and the log notes that the idle time was still billed.

Step 3: The router sees the nightly ETL is a production job, so it routes it to an ephemeral Job cluster. A fresh cluster is created just for this run, pays a small startup cost, runs the heavy ETL in isolation so no interactive user interferes, and is terminated the moment it finishes, so there is no idle cost at all.

Step 4: The router sees the morning dashboards are SQL analytics for forty concurrent users, so it routes them to the serverless SQL Warehouse. The warehouse starts almost instantly, serves the concurrent queries on the Photon-tuned engine, and bills only for the short burst.

Step 5: The demo totals the billed minutes per compute type and warns that running all three workloads on a single always-on All-Purpose cluster would have cost far more, because of idle time and collisions between the ETL, the developer, and the dashboards.

Final output:


sections.s6_takeaway:
Databricks offers three main compute types for three different kinds of work. All-Purpose clusters are long-lived, shared, interactive clusters that you keep running so people can attach notebooks and run commands, which makes them ideal for development, exploration, and collaborative analysis, with the trade-off that because they are shared and long-lived they cost money while idle and one heavy user can slow everyone, so you set auto-termination. Job clusters are ephemeral: the Jobs scheduler creates a fresh cluster at the moment a scheduled job starts, runs only that job in isolation, and terminates it the instant it finishes, so production pipelines do not interfere with each other or with interactive users and you pay only for the exact run duration. SQL Warehouses are compute endpoints specialized for SQL analytics and BI, running the Photon engine and tuned for concurrent queries, available as classic, which runs clusters in your cloud account, or serverless, which starts in seconds from a managed pool and scales concurrency automatically.

The discipline is to match the compute lifecycle to the workload. You develop and explore on an All-Purpose cluster because you want a warm, shared cluster and do not want to pay a startup wait for every cell. You run production jobs on ephemeral Job clusters because they are isolated, reproducible, and cost nothing when idle. And you serve SQL analytics and dashboards on a SQL Warehouse, preferring serverless for bursty BI because it starts instantly and scales with the number of users, though a bank may choose classic warehouses inside its own network for the most sensitive data because serverless runs outside the account's network boundary.

At the National Bank of India we learned this the hard way because we initially ran everything, development, the nightly ETL, and the analysts' dashboards, on one always-on All-Purpose cluster. The ETL collided with developers' heavy queries, the cluster sat idle and expensive during quiet hours, and a runaway dev job could starve everyone. We fixed it by splitting the workloads: developers stayed on a shared All-Purpose cluster with a thirty-minute auto-termination, the nightly ETL moved to an ephemeral Job cluster that spun up per run and tore down after so it was isolated and had no idle cost, and the bursty morning dashboards moved to a serverless SQL Warehouse that started in seconds, handled the concurrent users, and cost nothing overnight. That matching of compute type to workload improved both reliability and cost, which is exactly what the three cluster types are designed for.
